passage:
For decades, climate policy focused almost entirely on cutting emissions. Adaptation — adjusting to changes that are already unavoidable — was treated as an admission of defeat. That attitude has shifted. A 2021 review by Fischer and Adekunle found that 87 per cent of national climate plans now contain adaptation measures, compared with 34 per cent a decade earlier.

Adaptation takes many forms. Coastal cities build sea walls and restore mangroves; farmers switch to drought-tolerant crop varieties; hospitals prepare heat-wave protocols. Some measures are strikingly cheap. Painting roofs white, for instance, may lower indoor temperatures by up to four degrees Celsius at almost no cost.

Yet critics warn of what they call maladaptation: responses that reduce risk for one group while increasing it for another. Sea walls tend to deflect wave energy along the coast, so a wealthy district may gain protection at a poorer neighbour's expense. Irrigation schemes that protect this season's harvest can drain aquifers that would otherwise support the next generation.

Economists disagree about priorities. Thorne (2022) argues that every dollar spent on early-warning systems returns roughly nine dollars in avoided losses, and is therefore the obvious first step. Others counter that such figures are averages that conceal enormous local variation, and that communities are likely to reject plans designed elsewhere.

What most researchers do accept is that adaptation and mitigation are not alternatives. Without deep emission cuts, the pace of warming may eventually outrun any defence that engineers can build. Adaptation buys time; it does not buy escape.
stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Sea walls have proved to be the most effective adaptation measure available.

Adaptation is now a mainstream but imperfect response that cannot replace cutting emissions.
Economists have finally reached agreement on how adaptation budgets should be spent.

Biodiversity is usually measured by counting species, but many ecologists now argue that the count is a poor guide to the health of an ecosystem. What matters, they suggest, is functional diversity: the range of roles that organisms perform, such as pollinating, decomposing or dispersing seeds.

The distinction has practical consequences. A grassland may keep the same number of species for decades while quietly losing the large-bodied grazers that shape its structure. In a long-term study of Kenyan savannah, Mwangi (2019) recorded a 41 per cent decline in seed-dispersing birds even though the total number of bird species fell by only six per cent. The list looked stable; the machinery was not.

Redundancy offers some protection. Where several species perform the same task, the loss of one may be absorbed by the others, a property often described as ecological insurance. However, redundancy is unevenly distributed. Tropical forests tend to have many pollinators per plant, whereas island communities may depend on a single species, which makes them far more fragile.

Conservation funding still follows the older logic. Because rare species attract public sympathy and legal protection, budgets are likely to be directed towards them rather than towards abundant species that do most of the ecological work. Critics of this approach point out that the extinction of a common species can alter an ecosystem more profoundly than the loss of a rare one.

None of this makes species counts useless. They remain the cheapest signal available, and they are comparable across regions. The argument is simply that a number, on its own, describes rather less than it appears to.

explain_zh: 主旨題在雅思裡常考「作者的立場有多強」。首段 the count is a poor guide、末段 a number, on its own, describes rather less than it appears to，都是「不夠用」而非「沒有用」，所以選 B。A 過頭了，末段第一句 None of this makes species counts useless 直接否定；C 的 always 是絕對詞，原文用 tend to；D 時態與事實都錯，第四段說經費「仍然」流向稀有物種。技巧：先讀首段末句與末段，再刪掉語氣過強的選項。

In 2018 a team led by Petrova excavated a cluster of pits beneath a car park in northern Bulgaria and found something unexpected: 6,000 charred grape pips, arranged in layers that suggested repeated use of the site over at least two centuries. Radiocarbon dating placed the earliest layer at around 4,300 BC.

The find matters because it challenges a familiar story. Standard accounts hold that systematic grape processing began in the southern Caucasus and spread westwards only much later. If Petrova's dates are accurate, either the technique travelled faster than historians have assumed, or it was invented independently more than once.

Not everyone is convinced. Dating charred plant material is notoriously difficult, because older carbon from the surrounding soil may contaminate the sample. A rival team has argued that the pits were disturbed by medieval ploughing, which could mix material from different periods. Petrova accepts that disturbance is possible but notes that the layers show no sign of the vertical mixing that ploughing usually leaves behind.

Chemical residue analysis may eventually settle the question. Tartaric acid, a compound strongly associated with grapes, was detected in 12 of the 15 pottery fragments taken from the lowest layer. That is suggestive rather than decisive: the acid also occurs in a few other fruits that grow locally.

Archaeology often advances in this cautious way. A single site rarely overturns a consensus, but it can widen the range of explanations that scholars are prepared to take seriously — and, in doing so, direct the next decade of digging.
stem: What is the passage mainly about?
options: A Bulgarian excavation that has raised doubts about the accepted account of early grape processing
Evidence that radiocarbon dating is unreliable in every archaeological context
The damage that medieval ploughing has done to prehistoric sites across Europe
Proof that grapes were first processed in northern Bulgaria rather than the Caucasus
explain_zh: 主旨題要辨認「文章的強度」。第二段說 challenges a familiar story，第四段說 suggestive rather than decisive，末段說 A single site rarely overturns a consensus，整體是「提出疑問但尚未定論」，選 A。B 把第三段對碳化植物測年的個別困難誇大成全面不可靠；C 只是反方的一個論點，不是全文主軸；D 說成 Proof，與 suggestive rather than decisive 直接衝突。技巧：把每段第一句串起來讀一遍，主旨通常就浮出來了。

In 2018 a team led by Petrova excavated a cluster of pits beneath a car park in northern Bulgaria and found something unexpected: 6,000 charred grape pips, arranged in layers that suggested repeated use of the site over at least two centuries. Radiocarbon dating placed the earliest layer at around 4,300 BC.

The find matters because it challenges a familiar story. Standard accounts hold that systematic grape processing began in the southern Caucasus and spread westwards only much later. If Petrova's dates are accurate, either the technique travelled faster than historians have assumed, or it was invented independently more than once.

Not everyone is convinced. Dating charred plant material is notoriously difficult, because older carbon from the surrounding soil may contaminate the sample. A rival team has argued that the pits were disturbed by medieval ploughing, which could mix material from different periods. Petrova accepts that disturbance is possible but notes that the layers show no sign of the vertical mixing that ploughing usually leaves behind.

Chemical residue analysis may eventually settle the question. Tartaric acid, a compound strongly associated with grapes, was detected in 12 of the 15 pottery fragments taken from the lowest layer. That is suggestive rather than decisive: the acid also occurs in a few other fruits that grow locally.

Archaeology often advances in this cautious way. A single site rarely overturns a consensus, but it can widen the range of explanations that scholars are prepared to take seriously — and, in doing so, direct the next decade of digging.

passage:
Classical economics assumes that people weigh costs and benefits and then choose whatever serves their interests best. Behavioural economists have spent forty years documenting the ways in which this assumption fails — not randomly, but in patterns that can be predicted.

One of the best known patterns is default bias. When pension enrolment was automatic, with an option to leave, participation in the schemes studied by Halloran (2020) reached 91 per cent; when employees had to sign up actively, the figure was 38 per cent. The paperwork was almost identical. What changed was the effort required to do nothing.

Governments have been quick to apply such findings. So-called nudge units now operate in more than thirty countries, redesigning letters, forms and websites so that the desirable option is also the easiest one. Supporters point out that nudges are cheap and that they preserve freedom of choice: nobody is forced, and the alternative remains available.

Sceptics raise two objections. The first is ethical. If a government shapes choices without announcing that it is doing so, citizens may be steered in ways they would not endorse if they were asked directly. The second is practical. A 2022 meta-analysis found that the average effect of published nudges shrank considerably once unpublished studies were included, which suggests that the early results were inflated by selective reporting.

Even critics rarely propose a return to the classical model. The evidence that context alters decisions is too strong for that. The remaining argument is about who should be allowed to design that context, and how openly they should have to do it.

passage:
The idea that everyone needs eight hours of sleep has proved remarkably durable, although sleep researchers have been qualifying it for years. Requirements vary with age, genetics and even season, and a small proportion of people carry variants of the DEC2 gene that appear to let them function well on six hours or less.

What is less negotiable is timing. The body's internal clock is set largely by morning light, and it tends to run slightly longer than twenty-four hours. Without a daily light cue, most people drift later. Adolescents drift furthest: Okafor (2021) measured melatonin onset in 300 teenagers and found that it occurred, on average, two hours later than in adults living in the same household.

This has consequences for schools. When a district in Seattle moved its start time from 7:50 to 8:45, students gained 34 minutes of sleep on school nights and attendance improved, although effects on grades were modest and varied by subject. Sceptics note that teenagers may simply go to bed later once the pressure eases, cancelling out the gain.

Sleep quality is harder to measure than quantity. Wearable trackers estimate sleep stages from movement and heart rate, and their accuracy for deep sleep is limited; in laboratory comparisons they may misclassify as much as a third of it. Researchers therefore warn against treating a phone's nightly score as a diagnosis.

The safest summary is unfashionably vague. Most adults need somewhere between seven and nine hours, at roughly the same time each night, with light in the morning — and the variation around that average is real.

On a still summer night, the centre of a large city may be seven degrees warmer than the farmland around it. The cause is not simply waste heat from vehicles and air conditioning, although that contributes. Dark surfaces such as asphalt absorb solar radiation during the day and release it slowly after sunset, while tall buildings trap the outgoing heat and reduce the cooling effect of wind.

The consequences fall unevenly. Analysing 108 American cities, Ruiz and Tanaka (2020) found that formerly redlined neighbourhoods — districts once denied mortgage lending — were on average 2.6 degrees hotter than wealthier districts in the same city, largely because they had 23 per cent less tree cover. Heat, in other words, follows old maps.

Remedies are well understood. Reflective roofing, permeable paving, street trees and small parks all reduce surface temperature, and trees add the further benefit of transpiration. Yet planting is slow. A newly planted street tree may take fifteen years to cast useful shade, and the species that grow fastest are often the least tolerant of drought.

There is also a trade-off that planners rarely mention in public. Cooler, greener streets raise property values, which can displace the very residents the intervention was meant to protect. Some cities now pair greening projects with rent stabilisation for exactly this reason.

Nobody suggests that cities should be abandoned; density brings real climate advantages, including much lower transport emissions per person. The task is to keep the density and lose the heat, and that is an engineering problem tangled up with a political one.

On a still summer night, the centre of a large city may be seven degrees warmer than the farmland around it. The cause is not simply waste heat from vehicles and air conditioning, although that contributes. Dark surfaces such as asphalt absorb solar radiation during the day and release it slowly after sunset, while tall buildings trap the outgoing heat and reduce the cooling effect of wind.

The consequences fall unevenly. Analysing 108 American cities, Ruiz and Tanaka (2020) found that formerly redlined neighbourhoods — districts once denied mortgage lending — were on average 2.6 degrees hotter than wealthier districts in the same city, largely because they had 23 per cent less tree cover. Heat, in other words, follows old maps.

Remedies are well understood. Reflective roofing, permeable paving, street trees and small parks all reduce surface temperature, and trees add the further benefit of transpiration. Yet planting is slow. A newly planted street tree may take fifteen years to cast useful shade, and the species that grow fastest are often the least tolerant of drought.

There is also a trade-off that planners rarely mention in public. Cooler, greener streets raise property values, which can displace the very residents the intervention was meant to protect. Some cities now pair greening projects with rent stabilisation for exactly this reason.

Nobody suggests that cities should be abandoned; density brings real climate advantages, including much lower transport emissions per person. The task is to keep the density and lose the heat, and that is an engineering problem tangled up with a political one.

Photographs of floating rubbish have shaped public understanding of ocean plastic, but oceanographers have long known that the visible material is only a small fraction of the total. Estimates published by Calderon (2019) suggest that surface debris accounts for roughly one per cent of the plastic entering the sea each year. The rest sinks, is eaten, or is broken down into fragments too small to photograph.

Where the missing plastic goes is now the central question. Sediment cores taken from the deep Mediterranean contain up to 1.9 million fragments per square metre, and researchers have found microplastics in Arctic sea ice, in river deltas and in the guts of deep-sea amphipods. Some of it, unhelpfully, returns to land: sea spray can lift particles into the air, and they are then deposited by rain.

Clean-up technologies attract funding and headlines. Floating barriers can collect surface debris in places where currents concentrate it, and a single system may remove tens of tonnes in a season. Critics argue that this is a rounding error against annual inputs of around eleven million tonnes, and that barriers may also trap the marine organisms that live at the surface.

Most researchers therefore describe clean-up as a complement to, rather than a replacement for, reducing what enters the water in the first place. Redesigning packaging, improving waste collection in fast-growing cities and restricting deliberately added microbeads are far less photogenic, but they act further upstream — and upstream, in this field, is where the leverage lies.

explain_zh: 主旨題可用「首段的但書＋末段的主張」夾擊。首段 the visible material is only a small fraction，末段 upstream ... is where the leverage lies，合起來就是 A。B 與 a rounding error against annual inputs 相反；C 文章只說深海端足類腸道裡有塑膠，沒下無害的結論；D 顛倒了首段語氣，照片只是塑造了大眾印象，不是最有用的工具。技巧：主旨題看到 only、rather than 這種比較句型，往往正是作者的立場句。

Of the roughly 7,000 languages spoken today, linguists estimate that about 40 per cent have fewer than 10,000 speakers and are therefore considered at risk. Languages do not usually die because speakers are forbidden to use them, although that has certainly happened. More often they fade through a gradual shift, as parents who speak a minority language choose to raise their children in a dominant one because it offers schooling, work and status.

The loss is not merely sentimental. Small languages often encode detailed knowledge of local environments — names for plants, seasonal signals, navigation techniques — that may exist nowhere in written form. When the last fluent speakers of Yuchi or Eyak died, whole catalogues of observation died with them.

Revival is possible but demanding. Hebrew is the standard success story, although it enjoyed unusual advantages: a large literate community, powerful religious motivation and eventually a state. Maori and Hawaiian have recovered ground through immersion preschools, where children hear only the target language. Reported speaker numbers for Hawaiian rose from about 2,000 in the 1980s to over 18,000 by 2016, although researchers caution that self-reported fluency tends to be generous.

Digital tools cut both ways. The internet initially accelerated shift by making a handful of languages dominant online, yet it now supports keyboards, dictionaries and messaging in hundreds of smaller ones. Whether that is enough remains unclear. A language survives when it is used casually, between friends, about nothing in particular — and no application has yet found a reliable way to manufacture that.

Of the roughly 7,000 languages spoken today, linguists estimate that about 40 per cent have fewer than 10,000 speakers and are therefore considered at risk. Languages do not usually die because speakers are forbidden to use them, although that has certainly happened. More often they fade through a gradual shift, as parents who speak a minority language choose to raise their children in a dominant one because it offers schooling, work and status.

The loss is not merely sentimental. Small languages often encode detailed knowledge of local environments — names for plants, seasonal signals, navigation techniques — that may exist nowhere in written form. When the last fluent speakers of Yuchi or Eyak died, whole catalogues of observation died with them.

Revival is possible but demanding. Hebrew is the standard success story, although it enjoyed unusual advantages: a large literate community, powerful religious motivation and eventually a state. Maori and Hawaiian have recovered ground through immersion preschools, where children hear only the target language. Reported speaker numbers for Hawaiian rose from about 2,000 in the 1980s to over 18,000 by 2016, although researchers caution that self-reported fluency tends to be generous.

Digital tools cut both ways. The internet initially accelerated shift by making a handful of languages dominant online, yet it now supports keyboards, dictionaries and messaging in hundreds of smaller ones. Whether that is enough remains unclear. A language survives when it is used casually, between friends, about nothing in particular — and no application has yet found a reliable way to manufacture that.

When consultations moved online during the pandemic, the shift was presented as an emergency measure. Four years later, remote appointments account for a substantial and apparently stable share of primary care in several health systems, which has forced a more careful evaluation than enthusiasm alone allowed.

The evidence is genuinely mixed. For managing established conditions — adjusting medication for hypertension, reviewing a stable diabetic patient — trials generally find outcomes equivalent to face-to-face care at lower cost. A multi-site study by Lindqvist (2023) reported that 78 per cent of follow-up appointments could be conducted remotely without generating additional referrals. Diagnosing a new complaint is a different matter. Clinicians rely on cues that transmit poorly through a screen: skin tone, gait, the smell of a wound, the way a patient hesitates before answering.

Effects on access are the most contested question of all. Remote consultation clearly helps people who live far from clinics, work inflexible hours or have limited mobility. It may simultaneously disadvantage those with poor connectivity, limited digital confidence, or no private space at home in which to describe intimate symptoms. Whether the net effect narrows or widens inequality is likely to depend on which of these groups predominates in a given population.

Regulators are still adjusting. Rules on prescribing, cross-border licensing and record-keeping were relaxed quickly and have been withdrawn unevenly since. Meanwhile the strongest signal may be commercial: private providers have expanded fastest in precisely those specialities where remote assessment is easiest and clinical disputes least likely, which tells us something about where the model actually works.

passage:
Precision agriculture promises to apply water, fertiliser and pesticide only where they are needed, and only in the quantity required. The underlying technologies — satellite imagery, soil sensors, variable-rate applicators — are no longer experimental. Adoption, however, has been slower and far more uneven than vendors predicted.

Part of the explanation is simple arithmetic. Reviewing 62 field trials, Okonjo and Reiter (2022) calculated a median input saving of 14 per cent, which is meaningful but hardly transformative, and found that returns depended heavily on farm size. On holdings below 20 hectares, the equipment rarely paid for itself within its working life. Since roughly 84 per cent of the world's farms are smaller than two hectares, a technology that only pays at scale addresses a minority of producers.

Data ownership complicates matters further. Yield maps and soil records are commercially valuable, and supply contracts frequently grant the equipment manufacturer broad rights to use them. Farmers' associations in several countries have objected that this transfers bargaining power to suppliers who can see, in unusual detail, what each customer is able to afford.

The environmental case is nonetheless strong. Nitrogen applied in excess does not stay in the field; it leaches into groundwater and is released as nitrous oxide, a greenhouse gas roughly 270 times more potent than carbon dioxide over a century. Even a modest reduction, multiplied across the world's cultivated land, would matter.

The likely outcome is neither the revolution promised nor the failure critics predict, but a slow, partial adoption shaped as much by contract law and cooperative ownership as by the sensors themselves.

passage:
The cost of generating electricity from wind and sun has fallen faster than almost any forecast anticipated. The cost of storing it has not. This asymmetry now defines the engineering problem: a grid supplied largely by variable sources must hold energy across hours, days and occasionally weeks.

Lithium-ion batteries dominate the short end. They respond in milliseconds, which makes them excellent for smoothing minute-to-minute fluctuations, and grid-scale installations have expanded roughly fortyfold since 2015. But their economics deteriorate as duration lengthens: doubling the hours of storage roughly doubles the cost, because the expensive component is the cell itself rather than the container around it.

For longer periods, older and stranger options return. Pumped hydro still provides about 90 per cent of the world's storage capacity, though suitable sites are limited and permitting can take a decade. Compressed air, gravity towers, molten salt and flow batteries each suit particular conditions. Hydrogen is the most discussed and the least efficient: roughly 30 to 40 per cent of the original electricity survives the round trip from power to gas and back again, according to Berglund (2023).

That inefficiency may matter less than it first appears. Seasonal storage is used rarely, so its value lies in availability rather than throughput, and a system that sits idle for eleven months can still justify its losses if it prevents a winter shortfall. Critics reply that consumers will bear the cost of that insurance, and that demand flexibility — shifting when electricity is used — is cheaper than storing it. Both propositions can be true at once.

The cost of generating electricity from wind and sun has fallen faster than almost any forecast anticipated. The cost of storing it has not. This asymmetry now defines the engineering problem: a grid supplied largely by variable sources must hold energy across hours, days and occasionally weeks.

Lithium-ion batteries dominate the short end. They respond in milliseconds, which makes them excellent for smoothing minute-to-minute fluctuations, and grid-scale installations have expanded roughly fortyfold since 2015. But their economics deteriorate as duration lengthens: doubling the hours of storage roughly doubles the cost, because the expensive component is the cell itself rather than the container around it.

For longer periods, older and stranger options return. Pumped hydro still provides about 90 per cent of the world's storage capacity, though suitable sites are limited and permitting can take a decade. Compressed air, gravity towers, molten salt and flow batteries each suit particular conditions. Hydrogen is the most discussed and the least efficient: roughly 30 to 40 per cent of the original electricity survives the round trip from power to gas and back again, according to Berglund (2023).

That inefficiency may matter less than it first appears. Seasonal storage is used rarely, so its value lies in availability rather than throughput, and a system that sits idle for eleven months can still justify its losses if it prevents a winter shortfall. Critics reply that consumers will bear the cost of that insurance, and that demand flexibility — shifting when electricity is used — is cheaper than storing it. Both propositions can be true at once.

Students overwhelmingly prefer to study by rereading. It feels productive: the material becomes familiar, and familiarity is easily mistaken for knowledge. Cognitive psychologists call this the fluency illusion, and it lies behind one of the most robust findings in the field — that the strategies which feel most effective are often the least so.

Retrieval practice, which means attempting to recall material without looking at it, consistently outperforms rereading in controlled comparisons. In a frequently cited experiment, students who tested themselves recalled about 50 per cent more after a week than those who had reread the same passage four times, even though the rereaders had confidently predicted that they would do better. Spacing produces a similar pattern: sessions distributed over several days beat the same total time crammed into one.

Why the illusion persists is itself interesting. Retrieval is effortful and it generates errors, and effort is easily interpreted as a sign that learning is failing. Bjork describes such conditions as desirable difficulties: obstacles that slow immediate performance while strengthening durable memory.

Teachers should be careful before turning this into constant testing. The benefit comes from the act of recall, not from the grading, and frequent high-stakes assessment may raise anxiety enough to cancel out the gain — an effect that appears stronger among students who are already struggling. Low-stakes quizzing, flashcards, or simply closing the book and writing down what one remembers deliver most of the advantage.

Nor does retrieval practice replace understanding. Recalling a definition that one has never made sense of will produce nothing more than a durable memory of a meaningless string.

The claim that recommendation algorithms trap users inside ideological bubbles has become conventional wisdom, which is reason enough to examine it carefully. The evidence turns out to be much less tidy than the slogan.

Large-scale studies of browsing data repeatedly find that the average social media user encounters a wider range of political views online than offline, simply because online networks are larger and weak ties carry more surprising material. Bakshy's team reported that roughly 23 per cent of the political content shown to users came from the opposing side — more diverse, in other words, than a typical workplace conversation. The bubble, on this reading, describes ordinary social life rather than anything peculiar to technology.

Yet averages conceal the tail. A small minority of accounts consume extreme material at very high volume, and for those users recommendation systems do appear to accelerate the process, chiefly by lowering the effort required to find the next item. Ribeiro (2021) traced migration paths between channels and found consistent movement towards progressively more extreme content, although the study could not determine whether the system created the preference or merely served it.

There is a further complication that platforms rarely address directly. Feeds ranked by engagement optimise for reaction, and outrage reliably produces reaction. A system need not intend polarisation in order to reward it.

Sensible reform proposals therefore target mechanisms rather than opinions: offering users a chronological option, limiting the recommendation of untrusted sources to new accounts, publishing audit data for independent researchers. None of these is dramatic. Each of them is testable, which is more than can be said for the bubble metaphor itself.

Roughly 36,000 objects larger than ten centimetres are currently tracked in orbit, and perhaps a million smaller fragments are not tracked at all. At orbital velocities of about 7.8 kilometres per second, a fleck of paint carries the energy of a rifle bullet, and a loose bolt can destroy a satellite outright.

The concern is not simply the size of the present population but its capacity to reproduce. Kessler proposed in 1978 that above a certain density, collisions would generate enough fragments to cause further collisions, producing a cascade that continues regardless of whether anything else is ever launched. Two events have made the scenario concrete: the destruction of a Chinese weather satellite in a 2007 anti-satellite test, and the 2009 collision between Iridium 33 and a defunct Russian craft. Together they added more than 5,000 trackable fragments.

Mitigation rules do exist. Operators are expected to deorbit satellites within 25 years of the end of the mission, a period that some regulators are now cutting to five. Compliance has historically hovered around 30 per cent, partly because a satellite that has already failed cannot be commanded to move.

Active removal — capturing dead objects with nets, harpoons or magnetic docking plates — has been demonstrated in small trials but remains expensive, and every technique capable of removing a satellite is also capable of disabling one, which makes the diplomacy delicate.

The economics have the familiar shape of a commons. Each operator gains from launching; the cost of congestion is shared by all. Orbital slots, unlike fishing grounds, cannot easily be fenced.

Conservation once meant restoring a monument to the way it was believed to have looked at its finest moment. The Venice Charter of 1964 broke with that idea, insisting that later additions are themselves part of a building's history, and that any intervention must be both reversible and clearly distinguishable from the original. Repair, in short, rather than resurrection.

The principle is easier to state than to apply. When fire destroyed the roof of Notre-Dame in 2019, one camp argued for an exact replica in oak and another for a contemporary design in steel and glass. Both could quote the charter: the first preserved the appearance, the second the honesty. The replica won, which tells us something about how heritage decisions are actually made.

Digital documentation has changed the terms of the debate. Laser scanning can record a surface to within two millimetres, and the scans of Notre-Dame made before the fire proved invaluable to the rebuilding team. But a scan is a record, not a substitute; visitors do not travel across the world to stand in front of a file.

Funding introduces a further distortion. Because donors respond to recognisable icons, spectacular ruins attract support while vernacular buildings — the workshops, granaries and terraced houses that show how most people actually lived — decay quietly. Ahmed (2020) estimated that 61 per cent of heritage funding in the region studied went to fewer than 3 per cent of listed sites.

Preservation, in the end, is a series of choices about which past to keep, made by people who will not be there to see whether they chose well.

passage:
Conservation once meant restoring a monument to the way it was believed to have looked at its finest moment. The Venice Charter of 1964 broke with that idea, insisting that later additions are themselves part of a building's history, and that any intervention must be both reversible and clearly distinguishable from the original. Repair, in short, rather than resurrection.

The principle is easier to state than to apply. When fire destroyed the roof of Notre-Dame in 2019, one camp argued for an exact replica in oak and another for a contemporary design in steel and glass. Both could quote the charter: the first preserved the appearance, the second the honesty. The replica won, which tells us something about how heritage decisions are actually made.

Digital documentation has changed the terms of the debate. Laser scanning can record a surface to within two millimetres, and the scans of Notre-Dame made before the fire proved invaluable to the rebuilding team. But a scan is a record, not a substitute; visitors do not travel across the world to stand in front of a file.

Funding introduces a further distortion. Because donors respond to recognisable icons, spectacular ruins attract support while vernacular buildings — the workshops, granaries and terraced houses that show how most people actually lived — decay quietly. Ahmed (2020) estimated that 61 per cent of heritage funding in the region studied went to fewer than 3 per cent of listed sites.

Preservation, in the end, is a series of choices about which past to keep, made by people who will not be there to see whether they chose well.
